title: Are These Two Trees the Same Shape?

concept.title: Name every subtree shape by the sorted names of its children
body: Two rooted trees are *isomorphic* if one can be turned into the other by renaming the nodes and reordering the children of any node. In other words, they have the same **shape**; the node numbers and the order of the children do not matter. Comparing the trees by trying all orderings would be hopeless.

Give every possible subtree shape a small number (an *id*), assigned in the order of discovery, with this rule: the id of a node is decided by the **sorted list of the ids of its children**. A leaf has the empty list. Two nodes get the same id exactly when their subtrees have the same shape (by induction from the leaves up), and the sorting removes the dependence on the order of the children.

body.code:
ids = {}                                    # sorted tuple of child ids -> id (shared by both trees!)
for v in reversed(bfs_order):               # children before parents
    key = tuple(sorted(id_of[c] for c in kids[v]))
    if key not in ids:
        ids[key] = len(ids)
    id_of[v] = ids[key]
# the trees are isomorphic  <=>  id_of[root1] == id_of[root2]

body: The dictionary must be **shared** between the two trees, otherwise the ids would not be comparable. Sorting the children of all nodes costs O(n log n) in total, and the keys have O(n) numbers in total. No recursion is used, so a tree that is a path of 20000 nodes is no problem. This is the algorithm of Aho, Hopcroft and Ullman for rooted tree isomorphism.

statement: Two rooted trees are given by the parents of their nodes (0 for the root). They are isomorphic if the second can be obtained from the first by renaming the nodes and reordering the children of nodes (the roots correspond to each other). Print `yes` if the trees are isomorphic and `no` otherwise.
inputFormat: The first line has `n`, the number of nodes of the first tree.
The second line has `n` numbers: the parent of each node of the first tree (0 for the root).
The third line has `m`, the number of nodes of the second tree.
The fourth line has `m` numbers: the parent of each node of the second tree.
constraints: Both lines describe a tree: exactly one node has the parent 0, and following parents always reaches it.
A parent can have a larger number than its child.
The trees can be long paths.

examples.note: The first tree: the root 1 with the children 2 (which has the child 4) and 3. The second tree: the root 1 with the single child 2, which has two children. The roots have different numbers of children: no.
In the second tree the root is node 2, with the children 3 (which has the child 1) and 4. This is the same shape as the first tree: yes.

hints: Give each distinct shape an id, from the leaves upwards.
The id of a node is determined by the sorted list of the ids of its children; use one shared dictionary for both trees.
The trees are isomorphic exactly when their roots get the same id.

explanation: From the leaves up, each node gets an id decided by the sorted list of its children ids, with one dictionary shared by both trees. The trees are isomorphic exactly when the roots have the same id.
solution.complexity: Time O((n + m) log(n + m)), space O(n + m).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

def canon(par, ids):
    n = len(par)
    kids = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
    root = 0
    for v in range(1, n + 1):
        if par[v - 1] == 0:
            root = v
        else:
            kids[par[v - 1]].append(v)
    order = [root]
    for v in order:
        order.extend(kids[v])
    ident = [0] * (n + 1)
    for v in reversed(order):
        key = tuple(sorted(ident[c] for c in kids[v]))
        if key not in ids:
            ids[key] = len(ids)
        ident[v] = ids[key]
    return ident[root]

n = int(input())
p1 = list(map(int, input().split()))
m = int(input())
p2 = list(map(int, input().split()))

ids = {}
first = canon(p1, ids)
second = canon(p2, ids)
print("yes" if first == second else "no")
